title: Isaiah 52:1–12
context: Zion is told to awake and put on her strength and beautiful garments: historic Jerusalem, shake yourself from the dust, O captive daughter. Then the gospel turn: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news; the LORD has redeemed Jerusalem; depart, go out from there—not in haste, for the LORD will go before you.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Zion awaking and putting on strength, the captive daughter shaking off the dust, feet beautiful upon the mountains, Jerusalem redeemed, and a departure not in haste because the LORD goes before—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Isaiah 52:1–12.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Awake—This is a prediction and promise what she should do, that she should awake or arise out of her low estate, and be strong and courageous. Beautiful garments—Thy sorrows shall be ended, and thou shalt be advanced into a glorious condition. O Zion—O my church. Come—Either to molest thee, or defile thee. The uncircumcised—Heathens or infidels. Unclean—Nor any others, who are unholy. The dust—In which thou hast sat as a mourner. The bands—The yoke of thy captivity shall be taken off from thee. Sold yourselves—By your sins, without any valuable consideration paid by them either to you, or to your Lord and owner. Without money—Without paying any ransom. Egypt—Where they had protection and sustenance, and therefore owed subjection to the king of Egypt. And yet when he oppressed them, I punished him severely, and delivered them out of his hands. The Assyrian—The king of Babylon, who is called the king of Assyria. Without cause—Without any such ground or colour, by mere force invading their land, and carrying them away into captivity. What have I—Why do I sit still here, and not go to Babylon to punish the Babylonians, and to deliver my people? For nought—Without any provocation, or pretence of right. Howl—By their unmerciful usage. Blasphemed—The Babylonians blasphemed me as if I wanted either power or good will to save my people out of their hands. Shall know—They shall experience my power and goodness in fighting for them. In that day—When I shall redeem my people: which work was begun by the return of the Jews from Babylon, and perfected by the coming of the Messiah. The mountains—Of Judea, to which these glad tidings were brought, and from which they were spread abroad into other countries. Of him—Or, of them; the singular number being put for the plural. Returneth—In the days of the Messiah, God did discover and exercise his dominion over the world far more eminently than ever he had done from the beginning of the world until that time. Thy watchmen—Thy ministers, who descry the approach of this heavenly king. Eye—Distinctly and familiarly, their eyes beholding the eyes of this king of glory. They shall be eye and ear-witnesses of the words and works of Christ, and therefore their testimony shall be more certain and valuable. Bring again—When God shall complete the work of bringing his church out of captivity. Depart—Out of Babylon. Touch—Carry not along with you any of their superstitions or idolatries. Ye—And especially your priests and Levites, who minister in holy things, and carry the holy vessels of the temple, keep yourselves from all pollution. Not by flight—But securely, and in triumph, being conducted by your great captain the Lord of hosts. Rereward—So that none shall be able either to oppose you in your march, or to fall upon you in the rear.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 52:1–12)

reformed.quote: Awake, awake. He confirms the former doctrine, in order still more to arouse the people who had been weighed down by grief and sorrow; he addresses the Church, which appeared to be in a benumbed and drowsy condition, and bids her awake, that she may collect her strength and revive her courage; it is difficult to arouse those whose hearts have been laid prostrate by a sense of God's anger. Put on thy strength: formerly thou wast dejected, and wallowedst in filth; now prepare for a happy and prosperous condition, to which the Lord will restore thee. By the uncircumcised and unclean he means all irreligious persons who corrupt the worship of God; circumcision is nothing in itself unless there be added purity of heart. Shake thyself from the dust: let us not think that our liberty is in our power; it belongs to God alone to raise us from the dust and, by loosing our chains, to set us at liberty; the imperative has a more powerful tendency to arouse than plain narrative. Ye have been sold for nought; he has received no price, and is under no obligations to a creditor; the Babylonians have no right to detain you. Some explain it more ingeniously that Christ has redeemed us by free grace: this doctrine must indeed be maintained, but does not agree with the Prophet's meaning, who intended to correct the distrust of the Jews. If the Lord punished the Egyptians, much more will he punish the Babylonians, who have cruelly tyrannized over them. For the sake of his own honor the Lord preserves the Church. Therefore shall my people know my name: to know the name of the Lord is to know him from his word, which is his true image, and next from his works; the promises of God and the fulfillment of them are linked together by an indissoluble bond. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings: he speaks of the doctrine of salvation; this message is sent to the Church; Paul quotes this passage to prove that the preaching of the Gospel proceeds not from men but from God. Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; there will be silence during the captivity; when he restored the Jews to liberty, and employed the ministry of Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, these things were fulfilled; yet they ought to be continued down to the coming of Christ, by which the Church was gathered out of all parts of the world. Ye wildernesses of Jerusalem: to deliver the Church is God's own work. Jehovah hath made bare the arm of his holiness: we must begin with the deliverance which was wrought under Cyrus and bring it down to our own time. Depart ye: out of Babylon; he does not exhort the Jews to be clean when they shall be free, but so long as they shall be held captive; this doctrine relates not only to ministers of the word, but to all Christians, who are also called a royal priesthood. For not in haste shall ye go out: this deliverance shall not resemble a flight such as that of Egypt; they shall go away like conquerors; Jehovah will go before you and will assemble you.

verses.text: Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city; for there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean.
verses.arminianNotes:
Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city; for there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean. Wesley: Awake—This is a prediction and promise what she should do, that she should awake or arise out of her low estate, and be strong and courageous. Beautiful garments—Thy sorrows shall be ended, and thou shalt be advanced into a glorious condition. O Zion—O my church. Come—Either to molest thee, or defile thee. The uncircumcised—Heathens or infidels. Unclean—Nor any others, who are unholy.

Arminian hearing: the awake is a real prediction and promise, not a feint; historic Jerusalem, the holy city, is told she shall arise. Shared: awake; put on strength; beautiful garments; Zion; Jerusalem the holy city; no more uncircumcised and unclean. Carry 51:17: the city told to wake after the cup is now told to put on strength. Historic then gospel: the same Zion Wesley names my church. Do not force Isa 53 atonement onto this range; Wesley treats 52:13 as the beginning of a new prophecy. No millennial fight; no newspaper about later garments.
verses.reformedNotes:
Awake, awake. Calvin: he confirms the former doctrine, in order still more to arouse the people who had been weighed down by grief and sorrow; these things were necessary as spurs, that the doctrine might penetrate into their drowsy and stupified hearts; he addresses the Church, which appeared to be in a benumbed and drowsy condition, and bids her awake, that she may collect her strength and revive her courage; he repeats it a second time, for it is difficult to arouse those whose hearts have been struck, and even laid prostrate, by a sense of God's anger. Put on thy strength: formerly thou wast dejected, and wallowedst in filth and pollution; now prepare for a happy and prosperous condition, to which the Lord will restore thee. By the uncircumcised and unclean he means all irreligious persons who corrupt the worship of God and oppress consciences by tyranny; the mark of circumcision is nothing in itself, and unless there be added purity of heart is even reckoned uncircumcision; yet he does not object to viewing these words as applied to outward foes.

Reformed hearing: historic Jerusalem first, then the Church spurred from a sense of his anger. Shared: awake; strength; garments of beauty; no more access for the unclean. Carry 51:17: Calvin's raising from the grave is the same wake. Do not force Isa 53 here; Calvin does not pass to the Servant until 52:13. No dispensational chart of later cities. No open theism: the God who laid her prostrate also restores her.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear Zion told to awake and put on strength and beauty, the holy city no more entered by the unclean. Wesley takes Awake as a prediction and promise of what she should do—arise out of her low estate, strong and courageous—Zion as my church, the uncircumcised as heathens or infidels. Calvin takes the doubled Awake as spurs to a Church benumbed and laid prostrate by a sense of God's anger, strength contrasted with despondency, and the uncircumcised as irreligious persons who corrupt worship, circumcision nothing without purity of heart.

verses.text: Shake yourself from the dust and arise; be seated, O Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, O captive daughter of Zion.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shake yourself from the dust and arise; be seated, O Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, O captive daughter of Zion. Wesley: The dust—In which thou hast sat as a mourner. The bands—The yoke of thy captivity shall be taken off from thee.

Arminian streets: historic Jerusalem still in the dust of 51:23, the captive daughter told to shake it off—the yoke actually taken, not a feint. Shared: shake from the dust; arise; sit; loose the bonds; captive daughter of Zion. Carry 51:17 and 51:23: she drank; her back was the street; now she sits. Gospel still waits in the good news of v. 7 and the redeemed city of v. 9. No culture war about later dust; the point is the mourner's yoke coming off. Do not force Isa 53 onto this captive; Wesley does not.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shake thyself from the dust; arise. Calvin: he explains more fully the deliverance of the Church. When he bids her shake off the dust and arise, let us not on that account think that our liberty is in our power, so that we can obtain it whenever we think fit; for it belongs to God alone to raise us from the dust, to lift us up when we are prostrate, and, by breaking or loosing our chains, to set us at liberty. Why then the imperative? It has a much more powerful tendency to arouse than if he had employed plain narrative; therefore he declares that, when God shall have restored her to her former freedom, she shall come out of the mire. Sit, O Jerusalem: sit denotes a flourishing condition, contrasted with to lie, which denotes the lowest calamity; after ordering her to arise, he adds that she may sit—that she may no longer lie down, but may regain her former condition, and not be in future laid prostrate by enemies.

Reformed hearing: God alone looses; the command is a spur, not a claim that we raise ourselves. Shared: dust shaken; arise; sit; bonds loosed; captive daughter. Carry 51:23: the street-back now sits. Historic Judah first, then the Church God raises. No millennial timetable of later sittings.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear the captive daughter told to shake off dust and loose the bonds of her neck. Wesley takes the dust as that in which thou hast sat as a mourner, and the bands as the yoke of thy captivity taken off from thee. Calvin grants the same rising, then refuses to read the imperative as liberty in our power: it belongs to God alone to raise us from the dust and loose our chains; the command arouses; sit means she shall flourish and not lie prostrate.

verses.text: For thus says the LORD: "You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money."
verses.arminianNotes:
For thus says the LORD: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money. Wesley: Sold yourselves—By your sins, without any valuable consideration paid by them either to you, or to your Lord and owner. Without money—Without paying any ransom.

Arminian redemption: they sold themselves by their sins; the buyers paid nothing, and they shall be brought back without paying any ransom—historic Judah first, then gospel. Shared: sold for nothing; redeemed without money. Carry 50:1: which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Those who stay sold do not stay because no redemption without money was spoken. Do not force Isa 53 atonement onto this verse; Wesley's without money is no ransom paid, not the Servant's wound. No dispensational chart of later sales.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ye have been sold for nought. Calvin: this verse has been badly expounded by many who have chosen to enter into philosophical subtleties. He has received no price, and is under no obligations to a creditor who can claim them as having been purchased by him. I did not sell or make a conveyance of you to them; for nought were ye sold; and therefore I can justly claim you as my property. Do not reason on this matter by human arguments; for the Babylonians have no right to detain you. Therefore shall ye be redeemed without money: he sold and gave them up to their enemies for no other reason than because they had provoked him by their sins; there will be no greater difficulty in delivering them than in giving them up. Some explain it more ingeniously thus, that Christ has redeemed us by free grace. This doctrine must indeed be maintained, but does not agree with the Prophet's meaning, who intended to correct the distrust of the Jews, that they might have no doubt as to their being set at liberty.

Reformed hearing: God never conveyed them; Babylon cannot keep them; when he is pleased to deliver, no bargain is needed. Shared: sold for nought; redeemed without money. Calvin himself will not force Christ's free-grace redemption onto this verse as the Prophet's sense—do not force Isa 53 here. Carry 50:1. No open theism: the owner who gave them up can take them back.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear a people sold for nought and redeemed without money. Wesley takes Sold yourselves as by your sins, without any valuable consideration paid by them either to you or to your Lord and owner, and without money as without paying any ransom. Calvin takes the nought as God having received no price and being under no obligation to a creditor, so he can justly claim them; he grants they were given up because they had provoked him by their sins, but refuses the ingenious reading that Christ has redeemed us by free grace as the Prophet's meaning here, though that doctrine must be maintained.

verses.text: For thus says the Lord GOD: "My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there, and the Assyrian oppressed them for nothing.
verses.arminianNotes:
For thus says the Lord GOD: My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there, and the Assyrian oppressed them for nothing. Wesley: Egypt—Where they had protection and sustenance, and therefore owed subjection to the king of Egypt. And yet when he oppressed them, I punished him severely, and delivered them out of his hands. The Assyrian—The king of Babylon, who is called the king of Assyria, because it was one and the same empire which was possessed, first by the Assyrians, then by the Babylonians, and afterwards by the Persians. Without cause—Without any such ground or colour, by mere force invading their land, and carrying them away into captivity.

Arminian history: Egypt first, then Babylon under the Assyrian name—real sojourn, real oppression without cause. Shared: my people; Egypt to sojourn; the Assyrian oppressed for nothing. Carry 51:9: Rahab and the dragon were this Egypt; the same arm still delivers. No newspaper about later Assyrias; the point is the God who already punished Pharaoh. Do not force Isa 53 onto this sojourn; Wesley does not.
verses.reformedNotes:
Into Egypt my people went down aforetime. Calvin: commentators touch neither heaven nor earth; the Jews dream of three captivities, and Christians differ from them by thinking that this denotes a third captivity, which shall be under Antichrist, and from which Christ will deliver them. But the Prophet's meaning is quite different; he argues from the less to the greater by quoting the Egyptian captivity. If the Lord punished the Egyptians because their treatment of his people was harsh and unjust, much more will he punish the Babylonians, who have cruelly tyrannized over them. There was much greater plausibility in Pharaoh's claim of dominion than in that of the Babylonians; Jacob having voluntarily come down became subject to Pharaoh; far more base was the wickedness of the Babylonians, who drove the Jews out of a lawful possession. By the Assyrian he means the Babylonians, who were united under the same monarchy; he takes special notice of the Assyrian because he was the first that grievously distressed the Jews and prepared the way for this captivity.

Reformed history: Egypt the lesser title, Babylon the robber. Shared: Egypt first; Assyrian as Babylon; without cause. Calvin refuses a third-captivity or Antichrist reading invented onto this verse. Carry 51:9: the same Exodus arm. Historic then gospel: if Pharaoh could not keep them, Babylon cannot. No millennial camp fight about later captivities.

verses.text: Now therefore what have I here," declares the LORD, "seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Their rulers wail," declares the LORD, "and continually all the day my name is despised.
verses.arminianNotes:
Now therefore what have I here, declares the LORD, seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Their rulers wail, declares the LORD, and continually all the day my name is despised. Wesley: What have I—Why do I sit still here, and not go to Babylon to punish the Babylonians, and to deliver my people? For nought—Without any provocation, or pretence of right. Howl—By their unmerciful usage. Blasphemed—The Babylonians blasphemed me as if I wanted either power or good will to save my people out of their hands.

Arminian hearing: the LORD will not sit still—Babylon took them for nought and howled over them, and blasphemed as if he lacked power or will. Shared: what have I here; taken away for nothing; rulers wail; name despised all the day. Historic Babylon first, then gospel. Carry v. 3: sold for nought; now the name is despised because of it. Those who keep howling under rulers do not howl because he cannot go to Babylon. No culture war about later blasphemies.
verses.reformedNotes:
What have I here? Calvin: it is not reasonable that he should silently permit his people to be any longer oppressed; by these words he reproves, in some measure, his own delay: Shall I not stretch out my hand? If Pharaoh did not hinder me, though he was a lawful master, shall the violence of robbers hinder me? He enumerates the reasons which ought to move him to bring back the people: they are carried away for nought; they are constrained to howl without ceasing—to howl is more than to sigh or weep, extreme despair. The third and principal reason why the Lord will deliver his people is, that his name is continually exposed to the reproach and blasphemy of wicked men. For the sake of his own honor the Lord preserves the Church, and defends the pure worship of his name; by delivering his people, he will plead his own cause.

Reformed hearing: three reasons, the chief his own name. Shared: taken for nought; howling; name despised. Carry v. 4: if Pharaoh could not hinder, robbers cannot. No open theism: he is not surprised by the blasphemy; he names it as the reason he will act. Do not force Isa 53 onto this despised name; Calvin is still in Babylon.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear a people taken for nought, made to howl, and the LORD's name despised all the day. Wesley takes What have I as why do I sit still here, and not go to Babylon to punish the Babylonians and deliver my people; the blasphemy as if he wanted either power or good will. Calvin takes the same delay as reproved, then names three reasons, the third and principal that his name is exposed to blasphemy: for the sake of his own honor he preserves the Church and, by delivering his people, pleads his own cause.

verses.text: Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am."
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am. Wesley: Shall know—They shall experience my power and goodness in fighting for them. In that day—When I shall redeem my people: which work was begun by the return of the Jews from Babylon, and perfected by the coming of the Messiah. Behold—That all these promises are the words of the omnipotent, unchangeable God.

Arminian knowing: they shall experience the fighting; the redeeming work is begun at the return from Babylon and perfected by the Messiah—historic then gospel, shared christology, not a forced Isa 53 fork. Shared: my people shall know my name; in that day; I who speak; here I am. Carry v. 5: the despised name will be known. Those who do not know it do not fail to know because he never said Here I am. No millennial chart of later days; Wesley's day is Babylon's return brought to the Messiah.
verses.reformedNotes:
Therefore shall my people know. Calvin: at length the people must be redeemed by God, who cannot be unlike himself; if he redeemed the fathers, if he always assisted the Church, their posterity, whom he has adopted in the same manner, will never be suffered by him to be overwhelmed. To know the name of the Lord is to lay aside every false opinion, and to know him from his word, which is his true image, and next from his works. We must not imagine God according to the fancy of men, but must comprehend him as he declares himself to us. That it is I who speak: the verb to speak relates to the promises; Behold I relates to actual power; although now there be nothing more than that there sound in your ears the words by which I promise what is hardly probable, yet you shall speedily obtain it. The promises of God and the fulfillment of them are linked together by an indissoluble bond; he never promises anything in vain.

Reformed knowing: word first, then the work that confirms it; God cannot be unlike himself. Shared: know my name; I who speak; here I am. Carry the fathers he already redeemed. Do not force Isa 53 atonement onto this Here I am; Calvin is still answering Jewish distrust of liberty. No newspaper about later names.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear that my people shall know his name, that it is he who speaks, Here I am. Wesley takes Shall know as they shall experience my power and goodness in fighting for them, and In that day as when I shall redeem my people: which work was begun by the return of the Jews from Babylon, and perfected by the coming of the Messiah. Calvin takes the knowing as from his word, then from his works, God unable to be unlike himself, promises and fulfillment linked by an indissoluble bond, Behold I as actual power performing what the ears have heard.

verses.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, "Your God reigns."
verses.arminianNotes:
How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, Your God reigns. Wesley: The mountains—Of Judea, to which these glad tidings were brought, and from which they were spread abroad into other countries. Of him—Or, of them; the singular number being put for the plural. Returneth—In the days of the Messiah, God did discover and exercise his dominion over the world far more eminently than ever he had done from the beginning of the world until that time.

Arminian gospel: the feet are on Judea's mountains first; the tidings spread abroad; in the Messiah's days God reigns more eminently than ever—historic then gospel, shared christology. Shared: beautiful feet; good news; peace; salvation; Zion; Your God reigns. Carry 40:9 and 51:5: the arm the coastlands wait for is this reign. Those who hear no good news do not miss it because no feet came. Do not force Isa 53 atonement onto these feet; Wesley's Messiah here is the reigning God, not the marred Servant of 52:13. No dispensational chart of later mountains.
verses.reformedNotes:
How beautiful upon the mountains. Calvin: he confirms believers as to the certainty of the word of God, that they may be fully persuaded that they shall be restored to their former liberty. He does not now speak of every kind of doctrine, but of that which is adapted to consolation; beautiful and lovely is the approach of those who bring consolation from the mouth of God. Here he speaks of the doctrine of salvation, and consequently says that peace, happiness, salvation, is proclaimed. By peace he denotes a prosperous and happy condition. That saith to Zion: the beginning of that doctrine is that the kingdom of God may be erected among us; until he reign among us, we must be miserable; this message is sent to the Church; it cannot apply to heathens that know not God. Paul quotes this passage to prove that the preaching of the Gospel proceeds not from men but from God, and that the ministers who bring the message of salvation are sent by him; nothing is desirable but what comes from God; none but God can be the author of such a distinguished benefit.

Reformed gospel: consolation from God's mouth; ministers sent by God, not by men. Shared: beautiful feet; peace; salvation; Your God reigns; the message to Zion. Carry Paul's use: the same feet. Historic liberty first, then the Church's preached gospel. Shared christology: both camps hear the Messiah's reign and the gospel's feet. No millennial fight as Arminian versus Reformed; both hear God reigns.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear beautiful feet bringing good news of peace and salvation, saying to Zion, Your God reigns. Wesley takes the mountains as of Judea, to which these glad tidings were brought and from which they were spread abroad, him as also them, and the reign as in the days of the Messiah, when God exercised his dominion over the world far more eminently than ever. Calvin takes the beautiful approach as those who bring consolation from the mouth of God, the doctrine of salvation sent to the Church, not to heathens that know not God, and with Paul concludes that such preaching proceeds not from men but from God, who sends the ministers.

verses.text: The voice of your watchmen—they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion.
verses.arminianNotes:
The voice of your watchmen—they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion. Wesley: Thy watchmen—Thy ministers, who descry the approach of this heavenly king. Lift up thy voice—To give notice to all people of these glad tidings; and by way of exultation, to sing forth the praises of God for this glorious day. Eye—Distinctly and familiarly, their eyes beholding the eyes of this king of glory. They shall be eye and ear-witnesses of the words and works of Christ, and therefore their testimony shall be more certain and valuable. Bring again—When God shall complete the work of bringing his church out of captivity.

Arminian watch: ministers who actually see the king of glory—eye and ear-witnesses of Christ—while God completes the bringing of his church out of captivity. Shared: watchmen; lifted voice; singing; eye to eye; the LORD's return to Zion. Shared christology: Wesley names Christ here. Historic Zion first, then that testimony. Do not force Isa 53 onto this seeing; the king of glory returning is not the marred visage of 52:14. No newspaper about later watchmen.
verses.reformedNotes:
The voice of thy watchmen. Calvin: there shall be such a restoration of the people that the messengers shall venture boldly to proclaim it; they who speak of a doubtful matter mutter inaudibly; here there will be nothing doubtful or uncertain. The designation of watchmen is usually given to all Prophets, because they are placed on watch-towers to keep watch over the safety of the people. There will be silence during the captivity, because the voice of the Prophets shall not be heard; but when the Lord shall be pleased to lead forth the people, the mouth of watchmen, who were formerly dumb, shall be opened to proclaim that they are at liberty to return. Eye to eye: that is, openly. This extends indeed to spiritual conversion; but let us not on that account depart from the literal sense; when he restored the Jews to liberty, and employed the ministry of Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, these things were fulfilled. Yet at the same time they ought to be continued down to the coming of Christ, by which the Church was gathered out of all parts of the world. But we ought also to go forward to Christ's last coming, by which all things shall be perfectly restored.

Reformed watch: prophets silent in exile, then open; Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah first; then Christ's coming gathering the Church; then his last coming when all is restored. Shared: watchmen lift the voice; eye to eye; Zion brought again. Shared christology: Calvin also names Christ's coming. Do not invent a millennial camp fight here; his last coming is perfect restoration, not a chart. Carry v. 7: the same sent preachers.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear watchmen lifting the voice, singing, seeing eye to eye the LORD's return to Zion. Wesley takes the watchmen as thy ministers, who descry the approach of this heavenly king, eye to eye as their eyes beholding the eyes of this king of glory, they as eye and ear-witnesses of the words and works of Christ, and bring again as when God shall complete the work of bringing his church out of captivity. Calvin takes watchmen as the Prophets on watch-towers, silent in the captivity then opened to proclaim liberty, eye to eye as openly, fulfilled under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, continued down to the coming of Christ who gathers the Church, and forward to Christ's last coming, by which all things shall be perfectly restored.

verses.text: Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. Wesley has no separate lemma; vv. 7–8 still govern: glad tidings on Judea's mountains, ministers who descry the heavenly king, the church brought out of captivity.

Arminian singing: the waste places of historic Jerusalem are told to sing because he has actually redeemed that city—comfort sincere, not a feint. Shared: break forth; sing together; waste places of Jerusalem; comforted his people; redeemed Jerusalem. Carry 51:3: the LORD comforts Zion and her wastes like Eden. Carry v. 2: the mourner in the dust now sings. Do not force Isa 53 atonement onto this redeemed Jerusalem; Wesley has not yet reached the new prophecy he marks at 52:13. No millennial timetable of later wastes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Praise ye, rejoice together. Calvin: he exhorts believers to thanksgiving, but chiefly confirms them in the hope and confidence of this salvation, as if the actual enjoyment of it already called them to thank God for it. Although it appears unreasonable to prescribe a song of joy in the midst of grief, this form of expression is well fitted to arouse those who groan under sorrow, fear, and cares. Ye wildernesses of Jerusalem: he calls them wildernesses or waste places of Jerusalem, that, notwithstanding its ruin and destruction, they might still hope that it would be restored; this appellation is better adapted for shaking off fear than if he had called her prosperous. For Jehovah hath comforted his people: the Lord hath changed the mourning of the people into joy, and out of captivity hath made them free. In the promises of God, as in a mirror, we ought to behold those things which are not yet visible to our eyes. He hath redeemed Jerusalem: to deliver the Church is God's own work. And if we ought to judge thus of the redemption from Babylon, which was but of a shadowy nature, what shall we say of the spiritual redemption? Can it be ascribed to men without grossly insulting God?

Reformed singing: wastes named so ruin can still hope; Babylon's redemption God's work, and the spiritual more so. Shared: waste places sing; comforted; redeemed Jerusalem. Historic city first, then the Church only God can deliver. Carry 51:3. No newspaper about later ruins; the point is whose work the redeeming is.

verses.text: The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. Wesley has no separate lemma; v. 6 still governs: the redeeming work begun by the return of the Jews from Babylon, and perfected by the coming of the Messiah.

Arminian arm: the holy arm bared in the sight of the nations is the same fighting Wesley named in v. 6—historic return first, then the Messiah who perfects it, and the ends of the earth see. Shared: holy arm bared; eyes of all nations; ends of the earth; salvation of our God. Carry 51:5 and 51:9: the arm the coastlands wait for, the arm that cut Rahab. Shared christology: Wesley's Messiah belongs here as the perfecting, not as a forced 53-wound. Those who do not see this salvation do not miss it because the arm was never bared. No dispensational chart of later arms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jehovah hath made bare the arm of his holiness. Calvin: the comparison is borrowed from soldiers who stretch out their arms when they make ready for the battle; to make bare does not mean to hold out the naked arm, but to exert it. He calls it the arm of holiness because he intended to display his power for the salvation of the people; this implies a mutual relation between God and the Church which the Lord has consecrated to himself. True, he maketh bare his arm in the government of the whole world; but he does not call it the arm of holiness, as in this passage, when he renders peculiar assistance to his Church. Before the eyes of all nations: this deliverance shall be worthy of so great admiration that it shall be visible even to the blind. The extension of this magnificent spectacle to the very ends of the earth makes it evident that the Prophet does not speak of the return of the people, which would take place a few years afterwards, but of the restoration of the whole Church. This prophecy is maliciously restricted by the Jews to the deliverance from Babylon, and is improperly restricted by Christians to the spiritual redemption which we obtain through Christ; for we must begin with the deliverance which was wrought under Cyrus and bring it down to our own time.

Reformed arm: Cyrus first, then down to our time; neither Babylon-only nor Christ-only as a shortcut. Shared: holy arm bared; nations see; ends of the earth; salvation. Carry 51:9: the Exodus arm is this arm. Do not force Isa 53 onto the bared arm; Calvin has not yet passed to the Servant of 52:13. Historic then gospel, both required.

verses.text: Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD. Wesley: Depart—Out of Babylon. Touch—Carry not along with you any of their superstitions or idolatries. Ye—And especially your priests and Levites, who minister in holy things, and carry the holy vessels of the temple, keep yourselves from all pollution.

Arminian departure: out of historic Babylon, no superstitions packed; especially the priests and Levites who bear the temple vessels. Shared: depart; go out from there; touch no unclean thing; purify yourselves; bear the vessels of the LORD. Carry v. 1: the holy city no more entered by the unclean. The going is a real summons, not a feint. Do not force Isa 53 here; Wesley's vessels are the temple's, not the Servant's blood. No culture war about later uncleanness; the point is Babylon left behind.
verses.reformedNotes:
Depart ye, depart ye. Calvin: he now exhorts the people to be always ready to set out, and at the same time to bear their misery with patience. Before the time of deliverance arrived, they burned with extravagant eagerness to depart; but when the period of the captivity was fulfilled, they had grown languid, and there were few who returned to Judea. Touch not what is unclean: keep themselves pure from the defilements with which the Babylonians polluted themselves; not to pretend that they worship idols. He does not exhort the Jews to be clean when they shall be free, but so long as they shall be held captive, and even when their life shall be in danger. Be ye clean, that bear the vessels of Jehovah: this exhortation is especially directed to the priests and Levites, who, being standard-bearers, ought to maintain greater integrity; not that others have a right to pollute themselves. Yet I approve of the simple meaning, that the Levites and ministers of the temple are put, by way of eminence, for the whole of the people. This doctrine, therefore, relates in the present day not only to ministers of the word, but to all Christians, who are also called a royal priesthood, and not only are appointed to carry the vessels of the temple, but are themselves temples of God; on this account also Paul has applied this passage to the whole Church.

Reformed departure: clean while still captive; Levites standing for the whole people, now a royal priesthood. Shared: depart from Babylon; touch no unclean thing; bear the vessels. Carry 2 Cor 6:17 as Paul carries it. Historic vessels first, then the Church as temple. No millennial fight about later priesthoods.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear a doubled Depart out of Babylon, touch no unclean thing, you who bear the LORD's vessels. Wesley takes Ye as especially your priests and Levites, who minister in holy things and carry the holy vessels of the temple, keep yourselves from all pollution. Calvin grants the priests and Levites as standard-bearers, then takes them by way of eminence for the whole people: the doctrine relates not only to ministers of the word but to all Christians, a royal priesthood, themselves temples of God, as Paul applied this passage to the whole Church; and they must be clean while still captive, not only when free.

verses.text: For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard.
verses.arminianNotes:
For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard. Wesley: Not by flight—But securely, and in triumph, being conducted by your great captain the Lord of hosts. Rereward—So that none shall be able either to oppose you in your march, or to fall upon you in the rear.

Arminian march: not Egypt's scramble—securely, in triumph, the Lord of hosts as captain before and behind. Shared: not in haste; not in flight; the LORD goes before; the God of Israel your rear guard. Carry v. 11: the departure out of Babylon. Carry 51:10: the sea made a way for the redeemed. Historic then gospel: the same captain conducts the church. Do not force Isa 53 atonement onto this rear guard; Wesley's new prophecy begins at 52:13, which is the next unit, kept whole. No newspaper about later flights. No open theism: the captain already goes before.
verses.reformedNotes:
For not in haste shall ye go out. Calvin: he again magnifies that benefit of redemption, for it appeared to be incredible. He promises that this deliverance shall not resemble a flight such as that of Egypt; they fled by night out of Egypt, went out with haste, and Pharaoh pursued them; but the present case shall be totally different, and they shall go away like conquerors, so that none shall venture to give them any annoyance, so that this deliverance will be more excellent and wonderful. Jehovah will go before you: will be the leader of your journey. God was also the leader when he led them out of Egypt; but he did not at that time display his majesty as now, when, like a general, he brought back his army, after having vanquished his enemies. And the God of Israel will assemble you: there will be no scattering such as usually takes place under terror; they will march, as under banners, in a regular manner; God will bring you out as a band or army drawn up; none shall molest you; you will be assembled under God as your leader, that you may return into your native country.

Reformed march: not Egypt's night haste; a general after the victory; assembled, not scattered. Shared: not in haste; not flight; the LORD before; God of Israel gathering the rear. Carry v. 10: the bared arm is this general. After having spoken of the restoration of the Church, Isaiah will pass on to Christ at 52:13—Calvin's own seam; do not split 52:13–15 here, and do not force that atonement unit back onto 1–12. No dispensational chart of later marches.
